werk/chris-thile-not-all-who-wander-are-.text:
Not All Who Wander Are Lost is the third solo album by mandolinist Chris Thile and was released in 2001 on Sugar Hill. Even so, it is regarded as his first major record. In 2000 his group Nickel Creek had already gone platinum with a debut album, and that also brought attention to his own work.

The music builds on earlier work and is largely inspired by bluegrass and newgrass. Thile plays the mandolin and produced and mixed the record himself. He brought in many skilled players, including Béla Fleck on banjo, Jerry Douglas on dobro, Edgar Meyer on bass and Stuart Duncan and Sara Watkins on fiddle. The titles refer to Tolkien and to the comic strip Calvin and Hobbes: the album title comes from a poem in The Fellowship of the Ring.
werk/chris-thile-not-all-who-wander-are-.listen: Listen to Riddles In The Dark and notice how the mandolin takes the lead and the other instruments respond.

werk/chris-thile-stealing-second.text:
Stealing Second is Chris Thile's second solo album and was released in 1997 on Sugar Hill. He wrote all fourteen songs himself. He plays mandolin and bouzouki. Bluegrass musician Sam Bush produced the record and himself played fiddle and guitar. Others taking part include dobro player Jerry Douglas, fiddler Stuart Duncan, guitarists Russ Barenberg and David Grier and banjo players Alison Brown and Scott Vestal. Scott Thile plays bass.

The title song reached number 12 on the US bluegrass charts in 1997. The pieces are often short, between a minute and a half and five minutes, with exceptions such as The Game Is Afoot at almost seven minutes.
werk/chris-thile-stealing-second.listen: Listen to Stealing Second and notice how the mandolin takes the lead, with banjo and fiddle for company.

werk/chuck-berry-after-school-session.text:
This was Chuck Berry's debut album and only the second LP released by Chess Records. It came out in May 1957. With two exceptions, all the songs had already been released as 45 rpm singles. The recordings come from his first five sessions for Leonard and Phil Chess at the Universal Recording Corporation in Chicago, between May 1955 and January 1957. Wee Wee Hours came first, as the B-side of Maybellene. The last session produced School Day and Deep Feeling.

Accompaniment came from, among others, pianist Johnnie Johnson, bassist Willie Dixon and drummer Fred Below. On Deep Feeling the singer also plays a steel guitar. Several tracks were R&B chart hits: Too Much Monkey Business and Brown Eyed Handsome Man reached fourth and fifth place, and School Day topped the chart and reached number three on the Hot 100. Roly Poly and Berry Pickin' had not previously been on a single.
werk/chuck-berry-after-school-session.listen: In Deep Feeling, listen to the steel guitar, a different sound from the guitar this singer became known for.

werk/chuck-berry-one-dozen-berrys.text:
One Dozen Berrys is Chuck Berry's second studio album and was released in March 1958 on Chess Records. All the recordings came from Sheldon Recording Studio on South Michigan Avenue in Chicago, the studio that would later be called Chess Studios. The album is mainly a compilation: apart from five new tracks and an alternate take, all the songs had already appeared on singles.

New were Rockin' at the Philharmonic, Guitar Boogie, In-Go, How You've Changed and It Don't Take but a Few Minutes. There are also instrumental pieces, such as Blue Feeling. Low Feeling is the same recording as Blue Feeling, but with the tape played back at a slower speed. Well-known titles such as Sweet Little Sixteen and Rock and Roll Music are also included. In the band, Johnnie Johnson and Lafayette Leake play piano, Willie Dixon bass and Fred Below or Ebbie Hardy drums. In 2012 the album was released by Hoodoo together with Berry Is on Top on one CD.
werk/chuck-berry-one-dozen-berrys.listen: Listen to Blue Feeling, an instrumental piece, and notice how the guitar takes the lead here without vocals.

werk/chuck-berry-rockin-at-the-hops.text:
Rockin' at the Hops is the fourth studio album by the rock and roll pioneer Chuck Berry. It was released in July 1960 on Chess Records. Apart from four tracks, everything had already appeared on singles. The first single was Childhood Sweetheart with Broken Arrow, released in September 1959. Then followed Let It Rock with Too Pooped to Pop. The A-side reached number 64 on the Billboard Hot 100, the B-side number 42.

New were Down the Road a Piece, Confessin' the Blues, Betty Jean and Driftin' Blues. In the band, Johnnie Johnson plays piano, Willie Dixon bass and Matt Guitar Murphy electric guitar. The Ecuadors sing backing vocals and L. C. Davis plays tenor saxophone. The last two singles, Bye Bye Johnny and I Got to Find My Baby, did not chart.
werk/chuck-berry-rockin-at-the-hops.listen: Listen to Let It Rock and notice how guitar and piano together keep the accompaniment driving.

werk/chuck-berry-st-louis-to-liverpool.text:
On 18 October 1963 Chuck Berry was released from prison, where he had spent twenty months. In the meantime new groups had discovered his work. The Beach Boys built Surfin' U.S.A. on Sweet Little Sixteen, the Beatles played Roll Over Beethoven and the Rolling Stones had Carol on their first American album. Chess Records wanted to profit from the British Invasion and made a record with Berry aimed at young buyers: St. Louis to Liverpool, from 1964.

The album contains four of the five hits he had that year: No Particular Place to Go, You Never Can Tell, Promised Land and Little Marie, a sequel to Memphis, Tennessee. It also includes the B-sides of those singles, a B-side from 1960 and another recording of Merry Christmas Baby. There are also two instrumental tracks, including Liverpool Drive. It was Berry's first studio album on the Billboard chart, at number 124. Dave Marsh called it one of the greatest rock 'n' roll records ever.
werk/chuck-berry-st-louis-to-liverpool.listen: In No Particular Place to Go, listen to Berry's lyrics and guitar, and notice how a simple story about a car ride is told with great momentum.

werk/circle-alotus.text:
Alotus is the thirteenth album by the Finnish experimental rock band Circle. It was released on Klangbad, the label of Hans Joachim Irmler, one of the founders of the krautrock band Faust. Irmler is credited on the album as producer and co-arranger, and the album confirmed the bond between him and the group.

Four of the five tracks last well over ten minutes, only Northern Sky is shorter: a little over two and a half minutes. That last track also appeared on the compilation Klangbad First Steps. Singer Mika Rättö often wore a T-shirt with the cover of Faust's first album during performances.
werk/circle-alotus.listen: Listen to Northern Sky, the short track between the long pieces, and compare it with the sprawling Alotus.

werk/cliff-richard-cliff-sings.text:
Cliff Sings was released in November 1959 on EMI Columbia and was Cliff Richard's first studio album, his second album overall. It was recorded at Abbey Road Studios, with Norrie Paramor as producer and Malcolm Addey as engineer. In Britain no singles were taken from the record, which was normal before the 1970s. The album was recorded in stereo and mono, but at first released on LP in mono only.

This album began a pattern that lasted until the mid-1960s: the Shadows and Paramor's orchestra took turns accompanying the singer. According to the back of the sleeve, it was Addey who gave Paramor that idea. The Shadows' drummer Tony Meehan played on all the tracks with orchestra. The album reached number 2 on the British album chart. On the next album, Me and My Shadows, the Shadows played on every track.
werk/cliff-richard-cliff-sings.listen: Listen to Blue Suede Shoes and notice who accompanies the singer, the Shadows or the orchestra, and what that does to the character of the song.

werk/cliff-richard-listen-to-cliff.text:
Listen to Cliff! is Cliff Richard's third studio album and his fourth album overall. It was released in April 1961 on EMI Columbia and recorded at Abbey Road Studios, with Norrie Paramor as producer. The album reached number 2 on the British album chart and spent 26 consecutive weeks on the chart.

Officially no singles were taken from the record, and none of the 1961 singles is on it. Only Blue Moon was released as an export single. The repertoire consists mainly of covers of songs from musicals and from the popular music of the 1930s and 1940s. The Shadows' drummer Tony Meehan played with Paramor's orchestra. The album was later reissued, split across two EPs.
werk/cliff-richard-listen-to-cliff.listen: Listen to Blue Moon, which was released as an export single, and notice how an old standard sounds in the voice of a young rock singer.

werk/cliff-richard-when-in-rome.text:
When in Rome is a foreign-language album by Cliff Richard from 1965. It is his eighth studio album and fifteenth album overall. It contains mainly Italian songs, such as Arrivederci roma and Dicitencello vuie, and was recorded in Lisbon. One song, Maria Ninguém, is Portuguese.

The record was originally intended for Richard's Italian audience. It was also released in the United Kingdom, after his earlier album When in Spain had reached the top ten of the British album chart. This album, however, was received less well and was his first record to miss the charts.
werk/cliff-richard-when-in-rome.listen: Listen to Nel blu dipinto di blu (Volare) and notice how a British singer sings in Italian here.

werk/coldplay-a-rush-of-blood-to-the-hea.text:
After the worldwide successes of Parachutes and Yellow, Coldplay began work on a second album in London in September 2001, and later moved to Liverpool. Politik, the opening track, was written by Chris Martin on 11 September and recorded by the band two days later. By June 2002 the album was finished, but the band themselves did not think the result good enough and postponed the release. Late in the sessions Martin wrote a piano riff that became Clocks; that version was first put on a demo for a following album.

The album uses more electric guitar and piano than its predecessor, and was released on 26 August 2002. In My Place, The Scientist, Clocks and God Put a Smile upon Your Face became singles. The critical response was glowing, the album won, among other things, a Grammy for Record of the Year for Clocks, and earned a place on the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame's list of 200 Definitive Albums.
werk/coldplay-a-rush-of-blood-to-the-hea.listen: Listen to Clocks and notice the piano riff that carries the whole song.

werk/coldplay-mylo-xyloto.text:
Mylo Xyloto is Coldplay's fifth studio album, released in October 2011 by Parlophone. The band worked once again with producer Brian Eno, after Viva la Vida or Death and All His Friends. They recorded at The Bakery and at a new studio in London, The Beehive. At first they worked on two records, a restrained acoustic one and an electric one, but in the end it became a single album. Charlie Brown began as an acoustic song and took on a new form. Us Against the World and U.F.O. stayed understated.

It is their first concept album, a love story in an oppressed city, inspired by graffiti. The sound is more electronic and it opens with Hurts Like Heaven. Critics praised the optimistic tone, but some found it bombastic. Paradise and Every Teardrop Is a Waterfall received Grammy nominations.
werk/coldplay-mylo-xyloto.listen: Listen to Hurts Like Heaven and notice the electronic sounds and the processed vocals with which the album opens.

werk/coldplay-parachutes.text:
Coldplay began their debut album in the autumn of 1999. They first recorded in London with Chris Allison, then in Wales and in Liverpool with Ken Nelson, who produced most of the songs. A two-week recording turned into a seven-month project, because the band was also touring. Nelson had the group play more calmly, because live they sounded nervous and rushed. The result was a collection of moody, atmospheric songs at slow tempos, which critics placed alongside alternative rock and 1990s Britpop. Chris Martin wrote the song Yellow only after the first recordings had already been completed.

The record received positive reviews and shortly after release was at number one in England. It won a Grammy and a Brit Award. The album is dedicated to the mother of drummer Will Champion, who died two months before its release.
werk/coldplay-parachutes.listen: Listen to Yellow and notice the calm, slightly wistful atmosphere that characterizes the whole record.

werk/coldplay-the-scientist.text: On 11 November 2002 The Scientist by Coldplay from London was released, from the album A Rush of Blood to the Head. It is a piano ballad: Chris Martin begins alone on piano and the band does not come in until after the first chorus. In the video everything runs backwards, and Martin learned to sing the lyrics backwards. Coldplay grew into one of the biggest stadium bands of the twenty-first century.
werk/coldplay-the-scientist.listen: Hear the piano that carries the whole song. Only towards the end does the electric guitar come in.

werk/coldplay-x-en-y.text:
Coldplay's third album came about in a difficult period. The band worked on the record throughout 2004 and threw a lot away. Of sixty songs written, only eight remained, and the recordings with Ken Nelson were largely discarded. Manager Phil Harvey was temporarily away, so for the first time they were without his advice. In the end the band re-recorded the album with producer Danton Supple. The song Square One helped the band regain confidence. The record has twelve tracks, divided into an X half and a Y half, plus the hidden Til Kingdom Come.

Talk borrows the melody of Computer Love by Kraftwerk, but played on a guitar. Fix You begins as a gentle organ number and grows into a full finale. X&Y received good reviews and did very well worldwide, although the band themselves later became less satisfied with it.
werk/coldplay-x-en-y.listen: Listen to Fix You and notice how the song begins with only a soft organ and voice, and how guitar and rhythm then join in.

werk/coleman-hawkins-the-gilded-hawk.text:
The Gilded Hawk is an album by tenor saxophonist Coleman Hawkins, recorded at the end of 1956 and the beginning of 1957 and released on Capitol. Here he plays with an orchestra arranged and conducted by Glenn Osser. The line-up of that orchestra is not known.

The repertoire consists of well-known standards, such as Autumn Leaves, Stranger in Paradise, Everything Happens to Me and It Had to Be You. The string arrangements are soft and sugary. Hawkins mainly plays the melody, with great care for his tone. Critic Scott Yanow of AllMusic therefore considered the record one of the saxophonist's least essential: the strings weigh heavily on the music and little of note happens.
werk/coleman-hawkins-the-gilded-hawk.listen: Listen to Autumn Leaves: notice how Hawkins almost only follows the melody and lays his warm tenor tone over the strings.

werk/coleman-hawkins-the-hawk-flies-high.text: The Hawk Flies High is a 1957 album by tenor saxophonist Coleman Hawkins. He plays in a sextet most of whose members come from bebop: trombonist J.J. Johnson, trumpeter Idrees Sulieman, pianist Hank Jones and bassist Oscar Pettiford. Only guitarist Barry Galbraith and drummer Jo Jones had a different background. The repertoire is a mixture of original pieces by the band members and standards. Chant is by Hank Jones, Juicy Fruit by Sulieman, and Laura is a well-known ballad. Sancticity is by Hawkins himself. In this way a veteran of the swing era and a group of bebop musicians meet in one studio.
werk/coleman-hawkins-the-hawk-flies-high.listen: Listen to Laura and notice how Hawkins plays out the familiar melody on his tenor saxophone. Can you hear how the rhythm section quietly supports him?

werk/common-can-i-borrow-a-dollar.text:
Can I Borrow a Dollar? is the debut of the American rapper Common, who was then still called Common Sense. In 1991 a piece about him appeared in The Source's Unsigned Hype column, after which Relativity Records signed him. The label released three singles, including Take It EZ. With those he already had a solid reputation in the underground before the album was released on 6 October 1992.

Immenslope, later known as No I.D., and Twilite Tone produced the album, with additional work by the Beatnuts. The production is sparse, jazzy and relaxed, with samples, keyboards and drum breaks in the foreground. He raps in a sing-song style with a lot of intonation and fills his lyrics with wordplay and pop culture references. Critics called the album clever but little noticed. AllMusic sees it as an underrated debut that put Chicago hip hop on the map.
werk/common-can-i-borrow-a-dollar.listen: Listen to Take It EZ and notice how sing-song the rap sounds, and with what shifts in tone, over the relaxed, jazzy music.

werk/common-like-water-for-chocolate.text:
After One Day It'll All Make Sense, Common moved to New York. There, at Electric Lady Studios, he worked with the Soulquarians, a collective centred on, among others, Questlove, J Dilla, James Poyser, D'Angelo and Pino Palladino. Questlove oversaw the production. The album was released on 28 March 2000 on MCA Records and was his first record on a major label. The title comes from Laura Esquivel's novel.

The sound blends jazz, funk and soul with an Afrocentric bent. Time Travelin' (A Tribute To Fela) and Heat hark back to Afrobeat. Mos Def and MC Lyte take part, and as on the earlier records the rapper closes with spoken word from his father. A Song For Assata tells the story of Assata Shakur. The critical response was glowing. The album became his breakthrough, partly thanks to the video for The Light on MTV.
werk/common-like-water-for-chocolate.listen: Listen to Time Travelin' (A Tribute To Fela) and notice how the Afrobeat carries the song.

werk/common-one-day-it-ll-all-make-sense.text:
Common released One Day It'll All Make Sense on 30 September 1997 on Relativity Records. It was his third studio album, the successor to the highly acclaimed Resurrection. It was the first record on which the Chicago rapper officially dropped the word Sense from his name. It was also the last album with producer No I.D. until The Dreamer/The Believer in 2011.

Robert Christgau wrote in The Village Voice in January 1998 that this rapper has no aptitude for smooth earworms or broad appeal. According to Christgau he raps about black life and black manhood as most black people and young men really know them. His flow is not made for the dance floor, but it is complex and full. The track list features guests such as De La Soul, Cee-Lo, Erykah Badu, Black Thought, Q-Tip and Canibus.
werk/common-one-day-it-ll-all-make-sense.listen: Listen to Stolen Moments, Pt. 2 and notice how guest rapper Black Thought shares the song with the main rapper.

werk/common-resurrection.text:
Resurrection was released on 4 October 1994 on Relativity Records and was the second album by the rapper Common Sense. No I.D. produced most of it, as on the 1992 debut Can I Borrow a Dollar? It is the last album under his full artist name: afterwards he dropped Sense. The record is divided into two parts, the East Side of Stony and the West Side of Stony, after the street in Chicago where he grew up. Short interludes form a loose narrative about daily life on the South Side.

In I Used to Love H.E.R. he describes hip hop as a woman who goes astray through materialism. The song brought him to the attention of fans and critics, but also led to a feud with Ice Cube. The album received praise, although it sold poorly, and is often regarded as a classic. Rolling Stone placed it alongside Illmatic and Ready to Die.
werk/common-resurrection.listen: Listen to Pop's Rap, the closing track, and notice that here the rapper's own father is speaking, with spoken word and poetry.

werk/count-basie-and-his-orchestra-april.text:
April in Paris was the first record by Count Basie and his orchestra for the Verve label. It was recorded at Fine Sound in New York, in July 1955 and January 1956. The record was released in 1957. The arrangements came from, among others, Frank Foster, Ernie Wilkins, Neal Hefti and Joe Newman. Freddie Green, the orchestra's guitarist, wrote Corner Pocket.

AllMusic gave the record five stars and called it almost instantly a classic. The Rolling Stone Jazz Record Guide spoke of a commercial high point for this orchestra. The Penguin Guide to Jazz heard busy arrangements, tough solos and extremely precise timing.
werk/count-basie-and-his-orchestra-april.listen: In Mambo Inn, listen to the two extra percussionists who add to the orchestra's sound on this track.

werk/count-basie-basie-plays-hefti.text:
Basie Plays Hefti was released in 1958 on the Roulette label. On this album Count Basie's orchestra plays exclusively compositions and arrangements by Neal Hefti. The bandleader, Hefti and producer Teddy Reig had already worked together six months earlier on the album E=MC2. The bandleader himself plays piano.

All eleven pieces are by Hefti, among them Cute, Pensive Miss and Count Down. The orchestra includes trumpeters such as Thad Jones, Joe Newman and Snooky Young, trombonist Al Grey, saxophonists Frank Wess and Frank Foster, guitarist Freddie Green and drummer Sonny Payne. AllMusic gave the album four out of five stars and wrote that the orchestra was in top form.
werk/count-basie-basie-plays-hefti.listen: Listen to Cute and notice how the orchestra plays as one large whole, with the horns set against the rhythm section.

werk/count-basie-string-along-with-basie.text:
String Along with Basie is an album by Count Basie with a small group and a string orchestra. It was recorded in New York on 20 July 1959 and on 10 and 11 May 1960 and was originally released on the Roulette label. The pianist plays himself, with Freddie Green on guitar, George Duvivier on bass and Jimmy Crawford on drums. On some of the tracks we hear the tenor saxophonists Illinois Jacquet and Ben Webster, on others the flautists Herbie Mann and Frank Wess and a trombone section. Quincy Jones and George Williams wrote the arrangements.

The programme consists mainly of well-known songs, such as Summertime, Poor Butterfly, These Foolish Things Remind Me of You and Sweet Lorraine. There are also two blues: Stringing the Blues by Jimmy Jones and Blues Bittersweet by Quincy Jones. AllMusic gave the album four and a half stars.
werk/count-basie-string-along-with-basie.listen: In Summertime, listen to how the strings accompany the small group and what space the soloists are given.

werk/courtney-pine-modern-day-jazz-stori.text:
Modern Day Jazz Stories was released in 1995 by the English saxophonist Courtney Pine. In 1996 the album was nominated for the Mercury Music Prize. It also helped him win a Music of Black Origin Award for best jazz act.

Pine composed and arranged most of the pieces himself. There are also pieces by others: Don't 'Xplain is by Billie Holiday, In the Garden of Eden by Stanley Clarke and I've Known Rivers by Gary Bartz. In this way the record connects new jazz with older examples. The titles show that it is about stories: the album begins with a prelude, The Water of Life, and ends with an outro, Guiding Light. In between are titles such as The Unknown Warrior, a song for his ancestors. The source says no more about the recording and reception.
werk/courtney-pine-modern-day-jazz-stori.listen: Listen to Don't 'Xplain and notice how Pine plays a well-known song from the jazz tradition in his own sound.

werk/courtney-pine-underground.text:
Underground was released in 1997 on the Verve label. On this album the English saxophonist Courtney Pine plays jazz in which elements of hip hop are worked in. He himself plays soprano and tenor saxophone, bass clarinet and flutes, and wrote and arranged all the pieces.

He surrounded himself with American jazz musicians: pianist Cyrus Chestnut, bassist Reginald Veal, drummer Jeff Tain Watts, trumpeter Nicholas Payton and guitarist Mark Whitfield. To them are added DJ Pogo on turntables and singer Jhelisa. In this way a classic jazz line-up stands alongside a DJ, and that gives the album its own character.
werk/courtney-pine-underground.listen: Listen to Modern Day Jazz and notice how the turntable relates to the acoustic instruments: where do you hear jazz, and where hip hop?

werk/craig-armstrong-as-if-to-nothing.text:
As If to Nothing is the second solo album by the Scottish composer Craig Armstrong. It was released on 19 February 2002. For this album Armstrong worked with many guests from the pop world, including Bono of U2, the band Mogwai, Photek, Evan Dando, David McAlmont and Antye Greie-Fuchs. Singer Steven Lindsay, formerly of The Big Dish, also takes part.

The album blends orchestral music with popular voices and electronics. In Starless II Armstrong uses a sample of Starless by King Crimson. In Stay (Faraway, So Close!) Bono re-sings a song by his own band U2. He recorded that vocal in 2001 during the Elevation Tour. Ruthless Gravity, the opening track, was later used in the 2004 film Layer Cake and in an episode of Top Gear. Finding Beauty was covered by the band Escala.
werk/craig-armstrong-as-if-to-nothing.listen: Listen to Stay (Faraway, So Close!) and notice how Bono's voice blends with the orchestral accompaniment: what changes about the U2 song?

werk/craig-armstrong-the-space-between-u.text:
The Space Between Us is Craig Armstrong's debut under his own name and was released on Melankolic Records. Armstrong had earlier contributed to Protection by Massive Attack, and you can hear it. The opening track Weather Storm is a reworking of the track of the same title on that record, and Sly II is a reworking of Sly. Both versions of Weather Storm use a phrase from Autumnal, a 1972 work by Anthony Phillips.

Well-known guests take part on the album. Elizabeth Fraser of the Cocteau Twins sings on This Love and Paul Buchanan of The Blue Nile on Let's Go Out Tonight, a reworking of his own band's song. Balcony Scene is a reworking of Time Stands Still from the music for the 1996 film Romeo + Juliet, with elements of Kissing You by Des'ree and a quotation from the film.
werk/craig-armstrong-the-space-between-u.listen: Listen to This Love and notice how Elizabeth Fraser's voice relates to the music around it.

werk/craig-david-born-to-do-it.text:
Born to Do It is the debut album by the English singer Craig David and was released in August 2000 on Wildstar Records. After his work with the group Damage and with the garage duo Artful Dodger, Wildstar first gave him a development deal and then an album deal. Recording had already begun in 1999, before there was a label, in a small studio in Southampton. There he and Mark Hill wrote and produced most of the record themselves. Fill Me In was the last track to be completed.

The album blends 2-step garage with R&B, with acoustic guitars, strings and strong beats and bass. The lyrics are about love, complicated relationships and going out. With 7 Days and Fill Me In he reached number one in Britain. Critics received the record positively, although some found it a little monotonous. MTV included it in a list of the best albums ever.
werk/craig-david-born-to-do-it.listen: Listen to Fill Me In and notice the plinking keys and the measured strings: how do they sound together with the garage beat?

werk/craig-david-slicker-than-your-avera.text:
Slicker Than Your Average is Craig David's second album and was released on 19 November 2002 on Atlantic Records. After the success of Born to Do It, with which he also broke through in the United States, his style shifted towards a sound closer to American R&B than to the British garage of his debut. According to him the title can be read in two ways: as arrogance, but also as a sign of more calm and control.

He wrote World Filled with Love after being forced to stay for a week in a hotel room in New York following the attacks of 11 September 2001. The record leaked onto the internet before its release, which did not bother him much. Critics responded with mixed to positive reviews. The Guardian called it a remarkable record that at its best sounds curiously unique, while Blender mainly heard Timbaland-like productions, ballads and even Spanish guitars.
werk/craig-david-slicker-than-your-avera.listen: Listen to World Filled with Love and notice the lyrics: what message is the singer trying to convey, and how does the music support it?

werk/cream-disraeli-gears.text:
Cream's second album came about in New York. After their first American tour the band recorded most of it there in May 1967 at Atlantic Studios, in less than four days, because their visas were expiring. Felix Pappalardi produced, Tom Dowd was the engineer. Pappalardi turned the blues song Lawdy Mama into Strange Brew with new lyrics, the first track to be finished.

The band moved away from their blues roots and chose psychedelic sounds, as in Tales of Brave Ulysses and SWLABR. They are mostly short, self-contained songs, without the long improvisations of their live shows. The vocals were shared more evenly than on the previous record. Ahmet Ertegun at first thought the psychedelia nonsense, but gave in when Booker T. Jones and Otis Redding praised Sunshine of Your Love. The album contains those two hits, Strange Brew and Sunshine of Your Love.
werk/cream-disraeli-gears.listen: In Sunshine of Your Love, listen to the guitar riff that carries the song and to how the vocal lies over it.

werk/cream-wheels-of-fire.text:
Wheels of Fire is Cream's third album and was released in June 1968 in the United States as a double album: one record recorded in the studio, one live. Unlike Disraeli Gears, which was finished in a few days, this album took almost a year, in short sessions with producer Felix Pappalardi and engineer Tom Dowd. For the live side Pappalardi recorded shows in San Francisco in March 1968. By then the tension between the band members was running high.

On the studio record we hear exotic instruments such as glockenspiel, calliope and cello, alongside three blues songs in the usual line-up. Jack Bruce wrote, with poet Pete Brown, among others, White Room and Politician. The live side contains Traintime, Toad, Spoonful and Crossroads. The album was a great success and became the first platinum double album. Immediately afterwards it was announced that the group would split at the end of that year.
werk/cream-wheels-of-fire.listen: Listen to Crossroads and notice Eric Clapton's guitar in this live recording. Can you hear how he carries the song as a soloist?

werk/creedence-clearwater-revival-cosmo-.text:
Creedence Clearwater Revival's fifth studio album was released in July 1970 on Fantasy Records. The title refers to the shed in Berkeley where the band practised in its early years. Drummer Doug Clifford, nicknamed Cosmo, called that place The Factory, because John Fogerty had them rehearse there almost every day. Six of the eleven tracks were released as singles in 1970.

The album shows the roots of the swamp rock sound: R&B, soul, country, rockabilly and psychedelia. Travelin' Band is a salute to Little Richard. Lookin' Out My Back Door nods to the Bakersfield Sound and was written by Fogerty for his three-year-old son. There is also a seven-minute opener, Ramble Tamble, and an eleven-minute version of I Heard It Through the Grapevine. The album spent nine weeks at number one on the Billboard 200.
werk/creedence-clearwater-revival-cosmo-.listen: In Run Through the Jungle, listen to the jungle sounds at the beginning and the end: they were made with guitar and piano recorded backwards.

werk/creedence-clearwater-revival-green-.text:
Green River was released in August 1969 and was the second of three albums Creedence Clearwater Revival put out that year, between Bayou Country and Willy and the Poor Boys. John Fogerty wrote the songs, arranged and produced, and sang and played lead guitar. According to him the band played almost everything live together in the studio. They avoided the long jams of acid rock and chose tightly constructed roots music with a rockabilly edge.

The title song is about Fogerty's childhood summers at Putah Creek in California. Bad Moon Rising combines cheerful music with a dark lyric about impending disaster. Lodi tells of a musician stranded in a small provincial town. Commotion is read as a reference to the unrest in America. Green River and Bad Moon Rising both reached number 2 on the US chart.
werk/creedence-clearwater-revival-green-.listen: In Bad Moon Rising, listen to the contrast between the cheerful music and the threatening lyrics. Notice how light the band keeps sounding.

werk/creedence-clearwater-revival-willy-.text:
In 1969 Creedence Clearwater Revival released three albums, and this was the last, only three months after Green River. The band was by now one of the most popular in the world and had played at Woodstock. John Fogerty kept a tight grip on the reins, which caused friction with the other members. Originally the album was to be built around an old jug band called Willy and the Poor Boys. That idea soon disappeared, but it survived in Poorboy Shuffle and on the sleeve.

Fortunate Son is a protest song against the rich who support war without fighting in it themselves. Effigy targets President Nixon. It Came Out of the Sky tells of a farmer who finds a UFO in his field, in the style of Chuck Berry. There are also two songs connected with Lead Belly: Cotton Fields and Midnight Special. In 2020 Rolling Stone placed the album at number 193 of the 500 best.
werk/creedence-clearwater-revival-willy-.listen: Listen to Fortunate Son and notice the lyrics: who is being criticized here, and who does pay the price of the war?

werk/crosby-stills-nash-en-young-deja-vu.text:
It was the second album by Crosby, Stills & Nash and the first with Neil Young on board. They recorded it between July 1969 and January 1970 at Wally Heider's studios in San Francisco and Hollywood. The mood was dark: relationships were over, and David Crosby wept in the studio over the death of his girlfriend Christine Hinton. Most of the songs were recorded separately by the members, and the work took, according to Stephen Stills, about eight hundred hours. Carry On, by contrast, was finished in eight hours.

The album contains Teach Your Children, with Jerry Garcia on pedal steel, Our House and Woodstock, the Joni Mitchell song in an arrangement by Stills. Young contributed Helpless, and Country Girl, a composition of three fragments. The first reviews were mixed. Even so the album spent a week at the top of the Billboard 200 and remained the best-selling album of each of the four members' careers.
werk/crosby-stills-nash-en-young-deja-vu.listen: Listen to Teach Your Children and notice Jerry Garcia's pedal steel, which gives the song a country feel.

werk/culture-club-colour-by-numbers.text:
For their second album Culture Club again worked with producer Steve Levine at Red Bus Studios in London. New were the session musicians, including keyboardist Phil Pickett, who co-wrote two songs, and backing singer Helen Terry. The band drew on pop history. The melody of It's a Miracle is inspired by Matrimony by Gilbert O'Sullivan, and Church of the Poison Mind by Stevie Wonder's Uptight.

The album was released in October 1983, preceded by the hit Karma Chameleon, which reached number one in many countries. In England it reached first place. In America it spent six weeks at number two, behind Michael Jackson's Thriller. The reviews were generally positive. Rolling Stone saw in Boy George a first-rate blue-eyed soul balladeer. Later, critics regarded the record as the band's artistic and commercial peak. The four members themselves considered it their best work.
werk/culture-club-colour-by-numbers.listen: Listen to It's a Miracle and notice the melody, which is inspired by a 1970s pop song, Matrimony by Gilbert O'Sullivan.

werk/curtis-fuller-bone-en-bari.text:
Trombonist Curtis Fuller recorded this album on 4 August 1957 for Blue Note, which released it in early 1958. Alfred Lion was the producer and Rudy Van Gelder recorded the session. Alongside baritone saxophonist Tate Houston, a rhythm section plays with Sonny Clark on piano, Paul Chambers on bass and Art Taylor on drums.

The distinctive feature of the record is the combination of trombone and baritone saxophone. AllMusic describes them together as a thick, round-sounding front line, and calls the pairing unique. On some tracks one of the two horn players sits out. The sleeve was designed by Tom Hannan, the photographs were taken by Francis Wolff and Leonard Feather wrote the liner notes.
werk/curtis-fuller-bone-en-bari.listen: In Bone and Bari, listen to the combination of trombone and baritone saxophone: how do two low horns sound together as a front line?

werk/curtis-fuller-new-trombone.text:
With New Trombone, trombonist Curtis Fuller made his debut as a leader in 1957. He was only 22 years old at the time. The album was released on Prestige Records. He plays in a quintet with alto saxophonist Sonny Red, pianist Hank Jones, bassist Doug Watkins and drummer Louis Hayes.

The material consists of original compositions, such as Vonce #5, Transportation Blues and Blue Lawson, and two standards: Namely You by Gene de Paul and Johnny Mercer and What Is This Thing Called Love? by Cole Porter. On the CD, Alicia is a bonus track. Reviewer Scott Yanow of AllMusic called it a strong start to the young trombonist's career and thought all the musicians did well.
werk/curtis-fuller-new-trombone.listen: In What Is This Thing Called Love?, listen to how the trombone plays a well-known standard by Cole Porter.

werk/curtis-fuller-the-opener.text:
The Opener is trombonist Curtis Fuller's debut on Blue Note. He recorded it on 16 June 1957 and the label released it that same year. Fuller plays in a quintet with Hank Mobley on tenor saxophone, Bobby Timmons on piano, Paul Chambers on bass and Art Taylor on drums. Mobley does not play on A Lovely Way to Spend an Evening and Here's to My Lady.

There are six tracks. Fuller himself wrote Hugore and Lizzy's Bounce, Oscalypso is by Oscar Pettiford, and in addition the quintet plays standards by, among others, Gershwin. AllMusic found the record an extremely impressive whole.
werk/curtis-fuller-the-opener.listen: Listen to Hugore, an original by Fuller, and notice the sound of the trombone alongside the tenor saxophone.

werk/curtis-fuller-volume-3.text:
Curtis Fuller, Volume 3 was recorded on 1 December 1957, but Blue Note did not release the album until the end of 1960. The trombonist plays in a quintet with trumpeter Art Farmer, pianist Sonny Clark, bassist George Tucker and drummer Louis Hayes. Alfred Lion produced and Rudy Van Gelder recorded and mastered. Francis Wolff took the photographs and Nat Hentoff wrote the liner notes.

The album has six tracks, including Little Messenger, Quantrale and Carvon. AllMusic called it Fuller's third record as a leader for Blue Note and stronger than its predecessors, above all because of his writing talent. According to the reviewer it made Fuller a serious, mature voice on his instrument.
werk/curtis-fuller-volume-3.listen: Listen to Little Messenger and notice the interplay of trombone and trumpet.

werk/curtis-mayfield-curtis.text:
Curtis was released in September 1970 and was Curtis Mayfield's first solo album. He produced it himself and released it on his own label, Curtom Records. He was still a member of The Impressions and would not officially leave that group until 1971. The album sounds harder than his work with that group, with influences of funk and psychedelia, and deals with the political and social concerns of the time.

The singles Move On Up and (Don't Worry) If There's a Hell Below, We're All Going to Go showed the new funk style, the rest was softer soul. The album spent five weeks, not consecutively, at the top of the Billboard Black albums chart. AllMusic called it almost the Sgt. Pepper of 1970s soul.
werk/curtis-mayfield-curtis.listen: Listen to We the People Who Are Darker Than Blue and notice how the song moves between flowing soul and heavy funk.

werk/curtis-mayfield-roots.text:
Roots is Curtis Mayfield's second studio album and was released in October 1971. It received much praise from various magazines and is regarded as one of his best records and as a classic of 1970s soul. It reached number six on the Billboard Top R&B Albums chart.

AllMusic reviewer Bruce Eder wrote that the album takes off on some of the sweetest and most eloquent soul sounds heard up to then. He sings and plays guitar himself, with Craig McMullen on guitar and backing vocals by Leroy Hutson and Michael Hawkins. Johnny Pate and Riley Hampton wrote the arrangements. In 1999 a reissue appeared on Rhino with four extra tracks, including a demo version of Underground.
werk/curtis-mayfield-roots.listen: Listen to Get Down and notice how voice, guitar and rhythm section together create a relaxed soul groove.

werk/cyndi-lauper-a-night-to-remember.text:
A Night to Remember is Cyndi Lauper's third album and was released on 9 May 1989 on Epic Records. It was originally due out in 1988 under the title Kindred Spirit. When the song Hole in My Heart and the film Vibes turned out not to be successes, the project was adapted. Of the ten original tracks, eight remained, and A Night to Remember, Dancing with a Stranger and I Don't Want to Be Your Friend were added later.

The record produced a top ten single, but fell far short of the sales of her first two albums. The reviews were mixed to poor. According to AllMusic she was trying to become a mature singer-songwriter, which did not always work, except in I Drove All Night. Rolling Stone and the Los Angeles Times praised her voice, but found the material uneven. In interviews she herself calls the album A Night to Forget.
werk/cyndi-lauper-a-night-to-remember.listen: Listen to I Drove All Night and notice how her voice carries the song.

werk/cyndi-lauper-hat-full-of-stars.text:
Hat Full of Stars was released in 1993, four years after A Night to Remember, which had been poorly received and sold little. On this album Cyndi Lauper moved away from her pop sound and chose alternative music. Junior Vasquez, a dance music artist, co-produced, and many tracks rest on synthetic loops and percussion.

She wrote about social issues. Sally's Pigeons is about abortion, A Part Hate about racism, Product of Misery and Broken Glass about domestic violence and Lies about incest. A Part Hate was originally intended as an anti-apartheid song for her second album, but the label found that too political. The sleeve is inspired by a photograph of the actress Mary Pickford. Critics responded mostly favourably. Rolling Stone called it her most ambitious record, and Billboard spoke of a metamorphosis. The public response was cool, except in Japan and France, where it went gold.
werk/cyndi-lauper-hat-full-of-stars.listen: Listen to Who Let In The Rain and compare it with Time After Time, which Billboard said it reminded them of.

werk/cyndi-lauper-she-s-so-unusual.text:
She's So Unusual is Cyndi Lauper's first solo album and was released in October 1983 on Portrait Records. Earlier she had sung in Blue Angel, a band whose debut album was a commercial failure. Bankruptcy followed, and she kept working in shops and performing in clubs in New York. There she met manager David Wolff, who helped her get a contract with Portrait.

The music is mainly new wave, with influences of synth-pop and pop music. Six tracks were released as singles. Girls Just Want to Have Fun became a worldwide hit, and Time After Time became her first number 1 in America. With She Bop and All Through the Night she became the first woman to have four singles from one album in the American top five. Critics praised her distinctive voice. Lauper won two Grammys, including Best New Artist, and the album was later added to the American National Recording Registry.
werk/cyndi-lauper-she-s-so-unusual.listen: In Time After Time, listen to the restrained accompaniment and how the voice is given room to carry the emotion.

werk/cyndi-lauper-sisters-of-avalon.text:
Sisters of Avalon is Cyndi Lauper's fifth studio album. It was released on 16 October 1996 in Japan and on 1 April 1997 in the United States, on Sony. The title refers to the book The Mists of Avalon, which tells the Arthurian legend from the perspective of its female characters. She wrote many of the songs with Jan Pulsford, who had become the keyboardist in her band.

The sound combines electronics with traditional instruments such as guitar, zither, dulcimer and omnichord. The lyrics deal with indifference and discrimination. Love to Hate and You Don't Know target the media, Ballad of Cleo & Joe is about the double life of a transvestite and Say a Prayer about AIDS. Mother is an ode to Gaea. Critics were glowing, but the album was released late and sold poorly, except in Japan. The Songwriters Hall of Fame calls the title song a key song.
werk/cyndi-lauper-sisters-of-avalon.listen: Listen to Mother and notice the pagan atmosphere of this ode to Gaea.

werk/cyndi-lauper-true-colors.text:
After the enormous success of She's So Unusual, Cyndi Lauper wanted to approach her next record differently. She had first thought of Rick Chertoff as producer, but that collaboration went badly. She therefore made the album herself with Lennie Petze and wrote most of the songs. The album was released on 15 September 1986 on Portrait Records. The songs were meant to encourage listeners to love themselves a little more.

The title song True Colors, written by Billy Steinberg and Tom Kelly, is the best-known track and was covered by many artists. Change of Heart and What's Going On, with Chuck D, also reached the American top twenty. The album reached number 4 on the Billboard 200 and earned two Grammy nominations. The reviews were mostly favourable, although some felt the singer sounded less distinctive than on her debut. About seven million copies have been sold.
werk/cyndi-lauper-true-colors.listen: Listen to True Colors and notice how her voice starts softly and slowly gains strength, so that the song gives a comforting feeling.

werk/cyrus-chestnut-earth-stories.text:
Earth Stories was released in 1996 and is dedicated to the grandmother of pianist Cyrus Chestnut. He made the record together with producer Yves Beauvais. At first he thought of a sextet, but then he wanted to be the driving force himself. Alvester Garnett plays drums and Steve Kirby bass.

Chestnut wrote nine of the eleven tracks. The styles vary and, according to him, reflect his own history and his love of the blues. He called Cooldaddy's Perspective acoustic funk, with a horn section. Nutman's Invention #1 is played in ragtime style, and In the Garden is a version of a traditional spiritual. The reviews were warm. The Los Angeles Times praised his drive and technique, and the Washington Post called the record the best instrumental jazz album of that year.
werk/cyrus-chestnut-earth-stories.listen: Listen to Nutman's Invention #1 and notice how the piano sounds like ragtime, with a driving left hand.

werk/d-angelo-brown-sugar.text:
Brown Sugar is D'Angelo's debut, released in 1995 by EMI. The singer from Richmond, Virginia, began work on the first songs as early as the early 1990s at his mother's home with a four-track recorder and a keyboard. The recording followed in 1994 and 1995 in New York and in Sacramento, in Raphael Saadiq's studio. Unlike in the R&B of the time he used no famous producers: he wrote, played, arranged and produced most of it himself, with Prince as his example.

The sound combines gospel, soul and funk with hip hop beats. Fender Rhodes and Hammond organ carry the songs, with a tight bass and a seductive falsetto. Brown Sugar has the most hip hop in it, Cruisin' is a reworking of a Smokey Robinson hit and Higher closes with a choir of overdubbed voices. Critics praised the record as a turning point for neo soul, a term coined by manager Kedar Massenburg shortly after its success.
werk/d-angelo-brown-sugar.listen: Listen to Higher, the closing track. Notice how the organ, together with a choir of D'Angelo's own layered voices, builds a gospel-like sound.

werk/d-angelo-voodoo.text:
After his 1995 debut Brown Sugar, D'Angelo fell silent for almost five years. He suffered from writer's block, until the birth of his son in 1998 got him writing again. Voodoo was made in 1998 and 1999 at Electric Lady Studios in New York, together with drummer Questlove and other musicians around the Soulquarians collective. They watched old footage of Marvin Gaye, James Brown and Jimi Hendrix and then jammed for hours. That is how Africa came about, after they had spent an evening playing Prince.

The sound is looser and built more on groove than on his debut, with funk as its foundation and a lot of space between the notes. Untitled (How Does It Feel) became the best-known single. Voodoo was released in January 2000, went straight to the top of the American chart and won a Grammy for Best R&B Album. Writers see the record as a high point of neo soul. Rolling Stone later placed it at number 28 of the best albums ever.
werk/d-angelo-voodoo.listen: Listen to Africa and notice how the song keeps flowing as one long, loose groove, in no hurry to get anywhere.

werk/daddy-yankee-barrio-fino.text:
Barrio Fino is Daddy Yankee's third studio album, released on 13 July 2004. It appeared two years after El Cangri.com and was recorded in Puerto Rico between 2003 and 2004. He wrote all the songs and was executive producer. The lyrics deal with dance, sex, love, reflection and protest against political corruption and violence against women.

Gasolina, the first single, reached the top ten in, among others, Germany, Italy, Norway and the United Kingdom, and was the first reggaeton song nominated for a Latin Grammy for record of the year. Lo Que Pasó, Pasó reached second place on the American Hot Latin Songs chart. The album won a Latin Grammy for best urban album and helped reggaeton break through into the mainstream. Rolling Stone placed it at number 473 in 2020.
werk/daddy-yankee-barrio-fino.listen: Listen to Gasolina, the song that made reggaeton known worldwide, and notice the danceable rhythm.

werk/daddy-yankee-el-cartel-the-big-boss.text:
Daddy Yankee's fourth studio album was released on 5 June 2007 on El Cartel Records, through Interscope. It is the third part in a series after El Cartel from 1997 and El Cartel II from 2001. After the success of Barrio Fino he had signed with Interscope. Recording began in August 2006 at The Hit Factory in Miami and ended in April 2007 with the remix of Impacto with Fergie. He recorded 26 tracks in total.

The sound is hardcore reggaeton and Latin urban, with tropical rhythms, R&B and hip hop. Producers included Scott Storch, Luny Tunes, Tainy and Mr. Collipark, and guests were Akon, Fergie, will.i.am, Nicole Scherzinger and Héctor el Father. The first single Impacto won a Lo Nuestro Award for video of the year in 2008 and was on the soundtrack of Grand Theft Auto IV. The reviews were divided: some praised the variety, others found the reggaeton formula repetitive.
werk/daddy-yankee-el-cartel-the-big-boss.listen: Listen to Impacto and notice the infectious club sound that Scott Storch gave it.

werk/daft-punk-discovery.text:
Between 1998 and 2000, Thomas Bangalter and Guy-Manuel de Homem-Christo worked at Daft House, the studio in Bangalter's home in Paris, on the follow-up to Homework. That record had acquired many imitators, and the duo deliberately sought a different direction. They did not use standard house drum machines, but an Oberheim DMX, a LinnDrum and a Drumtraks, along with samplers, electric pianos and vocoders. They used Auto-Tune in a way it was not intended for. One More Time was already finished in 1998 and sat on the shelf for two years. Romanthony, Todd Edwards and DJ Sneak contributed.

The result is a concept album about the duo's youth, with influences of disco, post-disco, garage house and R&B. The album produced six singles, of which One More Time became the biggest club hit. Critics praised the innovation, and the album is regarded as an influential record for electronic and pop production.
werk/daft-punk-discovery.listen: Listen to One More Time and notice how the voice has been processed and how the dance record still sounds like a real pop song.

werk/daft-punk-homework.text:
Thomas Bangalter and Guy-Manuel de Homem-Christo had made two popular singles on the Scottish label Soma when an offer from Virgin followed in 1996. At first they only wanted to release individual singles, but after five months of work they had enough tracks for an album. They recorded it at home, in their own studio in Paris, quickly and cheaply. That is where the title comes from. They thought freedom important, so they paid for everything themselves and remained the owners of their masters.

Homework opens with Daftendirekt, part of a live performance in Ghent, Belgium. Da Funk blends funk and acid, Around the World revolves around a disco-style bass line and a persistent hook. Both reached number 1 on the American dance club chart. The record reached the top ten in England, sold more than two million copies and drew worldwide attention to French house.
werk/daft-punk-homework.listen: Listen to Around the World and notice how little happens: a solid bass line, a simple synthesizer melody and a hook that keeps coming back.

werk/daft-punk-human-after-all.text:
After the carefully constructed Discovery, Daft Punk wanted to do exactly the opposite. From September to November 2004 the duo made this album in six weeks, less than two of which were spent recording. Where Discovery was full of samples, there is only one sample here. The basis consisted of two guitars, two drum machines, a vocoder and an eight-track recorder. Thomas Bangalter spoke of an unpolished stone, and said the album was about fear and paranoia.

The songs are repetitive and minimalist, with heavy guitars and electronics. Robot Rock uses a melody from Release the Beast by Breakwater, and Technologic has a monotone voice reeling off commands. Make Love, by contrast, is calm neo-soul. Critics were mostly negative on release, but some appreciated the dark, experimental tone. After the acclaimed Alive 2006/2007 tour, many fans and critics took a different view of the album.
werk/daft-punk-human-after-all.listen: Listen to Technologic and notice the monotone, distorted voice reeling off commands against a tight guitar beat.

werk/daft-punk-random-access-memories.text:
In 2008 Daft Punk began work on new songs in Paris, but the duo were dissatisfied with the sampling and looping of earlier albums. After the Tron: Legacy soundtrack they chose live musicians. Through Chris Caswell a group of experienced session musicians was brought together: we wanted to do what we did with machines and samplers, but with people, said Thomas Bangalter. The album was released on 17 May 2013 and was recorded in secret between 2008 and 2012 in studios in California, New York and Paris.

It is a tribute to American music of the late 1970s and early 1980s. It blends disco, progressive rock and pop, with contributions from, among others, Nile Rodgers, Giorgio Moroder, Pharrell Williams and Chilly Gonzales. Only the closing track Contact contains a sample. Get Lucky reached number 1 in more than thirty countries. The album won the Grammy for Album of the Year in 2014.
werk/daft-punk-random-access-memories.listen: Listen to Giorgio by Moroder and notice the story of his life that Giorgio Moroder himself tells, and what the music around it does.

werk/daler-mehndi-bolo-ta-ra-ra.text:
Bolo Ta Ra Ra.. is the 1995 debut of the Punjabi singer Daler Mehndi, who sings bhangra. The record was first released on cassette on 23 January 1995 and on CD on 1 September of that year. Jawahar Wattal produced and composed, Ravi Pawar made the arrangements. The recording was done digitally at Adcamp in Delhi, by S.C. Chawla.

The album is regarded as the best-selling Indian pop record outside film: twenty million copies are said to have been sold, more than a million in Kerala alone. Alongside the music, the visuals also contributed to its success. Kanchan Sachdev did the choreography and Ken Ghosh made the video clip.
werk/daler-mehndi-bolo-ta-ra-ra.listen: In Bolo Ta Ra Ra, listen to how rhythm and voice together make the song danceable.

werk/daniel-lohues-allennig.text: On 27 March 2006 Allennig was released, the first solo album by Daniël Lohues, known from the band Skik. Allennig is Drents for alone: Lohues sings in his own regional language, calmly and personally. More instalments followed, and Allennig II reached the top 15 of the album chart in 2008. Lohues showed that a regional language is also suited to quiet, personal songs.
werk/daniel-lohues-allennig.listen: Hear Lohues's calm voice and try to follow the Drents lyrics.

werk/danny-elfman-so-lo.text:
So-Lo is Danny Elfman's debut as a solo artist, released in 1984 by MCA. Oingo Boingo had just been dropped by I.R.S. Records, and MCA offered Elfman a solo contract. The record was made mainly by him, but the band members play on it, and Flea of the newly formed Red Hot Chili Peppers plays additional bass. It was the last record with bassist Kerry Hatch and keyboardist Richard Gibbs.

Elfman saw the album as a chance to experiment with slower tempos and ballads. A song like Gratitude began as loose ideas that the band worked out in the studio. Cool City and Lightning date from the sessions for Good for Your Soul. The first vinyl and cassette version has a different mix of Gratitude, with a spoken verse.
werk/danny-elfman-so-lo.listen: Listen to Gratitude, the opening track, and notice the synthesizers and the slower tempo.
